sources.name: University of Nevada,Reno — 2018 project-owner SAM100 deployment report
Clark Construction — Superstructure Winter2015 firsthand SAM100 project report

highlights: Robotic arm applies mortar and lays bricks with laser guidance
Programmed brick patterns support long, uninterrupted wall sections
Human crews handle setup, material loading, finishing, corners and openings

Clark’s Winter 2015 project newsletter documents SAM100 placing approximately 12,000 bricks at the Lab School of Washington alongside Construction Robotics and masonry crews. This is a dated contractor deployment report, not an independent universal productivity test or a claim of current availability.

The Clark report describes a conveyor pick station, measurement of brick height/width with out-of-spec bricks rejected, mortar application and laser-referenced placement. The capability is documented for that installation and is not proof of autonomous navigation around an unprepared jobsite.

The August 22, 2018 University of Nevada report quotes 200-250 bricks per hour and separately observes about eight seconds per brick. Cycle arithmetic does not establish sustained 450-per-hour or full-shift output; these are historical project claims, not current universal ratings.

Crews remain responsible for scaffold/system setup, programming, material loading, row alignment and joint finishing. The 2018 account assigns the first five feet, corners and window/door interruptions to manual masons; workforce-equivalence and schedule-saving quotes are not general labor-replacement guarantees.

before.description: Historical semi-automated bricklaying robot documented on the University of Nevada, Reno Arts Building project in August 2018. The documented deployment does not establish current sales or support.

companyFocus.name: Construction Robotics
companyFocus.role: Historical programmed masonry robot and current hand-guided construction lift-assist equipment
highlights: Historical SAM100 bricklaying is documented by contractor Clark in Winter 2015 and project owner University of Nevada in 2018. Today’s manufacturer catalogue emphasizes MULE lift assistance; a missing SAM route does not by itself prove discontinuation or current sales. Construction Robotics remains distinct from Advanced Construction Robotics.

The current range names MZ100 and ML150. The manufacturer describes workers guiding placement directly with their hands. Support categories also name ML150S - Solar MULE; its exact independent configuration remains unreviewed. Masonry, manufacturing, solar, retaining-wall and form-panel applications do not create additional autonomous robot models.

The MZ100 sheet distinguishes three-link 367 kg/12 ft reach and two-link 340 kg/8 ft reach, with 100 lb/45 kg lifting capacity in both columns. These are hand-guided lift configurations, not SAM100 specifications. Its width pair 1 ft 10 in/0.81 m is an unresolved unit mismatch, not a silently corrected dimension.

The overview gives up to 30 hours operation and 3 hours charging, while the MZ100 page/specification give up to 32 hours and full charge in as little as 3.5 hours. Exact revision/test mapping remains unresolved. Conditional up-to-ten-year battery service life and 5000+ cycles per charge are separate from operating duration; belt speed is not autonomous vehicle speed.

Displayed 1465 USD/month assumes five-year financing at 7% for the MULE arm, subject to customer approval and changing rates. This is not a complete-system purchase price or SAM100 offer. IoT subscription availability, special grippers and custom applications retain their own configuration scope.

Productivity, worker-safety, insurance, profitability and weather-proof language are manufacturer claims without independently verified universal outcomes or a numeric ingress rating. The company’s NSF funding statement includes its own non-endorsement disclaimer; funding is not certification of safety or exclusive superiority.
